description: We are building "Earth Information Jukebox," a project that merges global data with creative tech to turn the planet's information into an immersive audiovisual experience. Our team brings a strong foundation in hardware aesthetics, conceptual design, and AI sound generation. We are looking for passionate full-stack developers and data visualization wizards to help bring our interactive elements to life. Join us if you want to geek out, build something unique, and give the Earth a voice!
summary: Frequency_Vista lets you hear NASA’s Earth data. A scan sweeps across the world map from west to east, and the picture turns into live sound: higher notes for the north, lower for the south, and louder where there is more light or warmer water. We built it for the Earth Information Jukebox challenge, using NASA’s night lights from 2012 to 2023 and global sea surface temperature. You can play one date, or compare 2012 with a later year and hear how the planet changed. Most NASA Earth data is pictures and video, which leaves blind and low-vision people out. We wanted them to explore the same data, so the whole app works by keyboard and with screen readers, and every sound follows a published rule.
details:
What it does: Frequency_Vista is a web app that turns NASA Earth images into sound as you listen. You choose a dataset (Night Lights or Sea Surface Temperature), a date, a speed and a volume, then press play. A scan line crosses the map from west to east over 16 seconds. In compare mode it plays the first date, then a later one, with one cue tone for the first scan and two for the second.

How it works: The map is split into 12 latitude bands (70°N to 50°S) and 256 steps from west to east. Latitude sets the pitch, in a musical scale, from 110 Hz in the south to about 523 Hz in the north. The brightness of lights, or the temperature read from NASA’s colour bar, sets the loudness. Longitude sets the time and the left-to-right stereo position. Bright clusters and warm-water regions ring as bells. All the scales are fixed, so 2012 and 2023 are measured with the same ruler.

Why rules, not machine learning: A blind listener can’t check the sound against the map, so each sound has to trace back to a formula. Nothing is invented, and the same data always gives the same notes.

Accessibility: One vertical menu runs from the keyboard: up and down choose a control, left and right change it, and P plays. Every step has a tick, and a low thud marks each end. The app speaks what it is about to play and starts the sound only after it finishes, so speech never talks over the data. It works with screen readers, and there are on-screen buttons for low-vision users.

Tools: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with the Web Audio API for live sound and canvas pixel analysis in the browser. Python and OpenCV for preparing frames offline. VS Code, GitHub and GitHub Pages.

What we considered: We masked the year label printed in NASA’s video so text never became data. We checked that grey land isn’t read as city lights. We kept the speech off by default so it doesn’t clash with a user’s own screen reader. We also know the limits: NASA’s frames are display-stretched, so the sound shows patterns, not exact values, and the temperatures are approximate.

Impact: Blind and low-vision people can explore NASA’s data for themselves. The same approach can carry to more datasets, and it can help teachers and science outreach too
